beats.say: In 1745 the Jacobite army marched not for a crown, but to retrieve a secret French gold stash near Inverness.
Charles Edward Stuart, the 'Young Pretender', hid treasure in a cairn on Ben Nevis, hoping clans would fund the campaign.
When troops discovered the plot, they seized the cairn, but the gold vanished overnight, sparking rumors of a supernatural guardian.
Charles claimed sabotage by English, yet letters later showed he had spent part of loot to bribe French officers.
The Jacobite defeat at Culloden on April 16, 1746, was hastened when soldiers, starving, raided gold, causing chaos in ranks.
Survivors later whispered that the gold's curse haunted the battlefield, its phantom clinking heard by the defeated Highlanders.
Decades later, a 1792 Scottish antiquarian uncovered an iron chest near Fort William, but it contained only empty pewter plates.
Historians now believe the true treasure was a cache of French codes that could have altered alliances.
The codes resurfaced in 1840 when a French diplomat in London sold them to the British Museum for a pittance.
So the story of Charles Edward Stuart isn't a lost crown, but an espionage gamble that reshaped the Jacobite cause.
